findings.claim: '...how to balance justice with compassion. the specification identifies four main categories of reasons for crime.'
findings.truth: The sentence starts with a lower-case 'the'.

findings.claim: 'The Bible warns: “The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10).' The knowledge check repeats the wording.
findings.truth: The NIV reads 'For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil'; the KJV reads 'the love of money is the root of all evil'. The published hybrid matches neither.

findings.claim: Revision tip: 'The question ‘can it ever be good to cause suffering?’ is a common exam topic.'
findings.truth: An unevidenced claim about how often a topic is set. The question is named in the course content, which is the checkable statement.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.5 Theme E - 'whether it can ever be good to cause suffering'

findings.claim: Question 2 in lessons 1, 2, 4 and 5 is labelled '1 mark - Give/Name' but its mark scheme awards two marks ('up to 2 marks ... [2 marks]' in lessons 1 and 2; '[1 mark for each correct point, maximum 2 marks]' in lesson 4; 'Any two of the following, 1 mark each' in lesson 5).
findings.truth: One five-part question is set per theme and the marks are 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12. There is no 2-mark part, so a 1-mark question takes one point. The label and the scheme also contradicted each other.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Component 2: Thematic studies - 'marks will be allocated as follows; 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12'; confirmed on the board's live scheme-of-assessment page

findings.claim: The death penalty 'was abolished in the UK in 1965 but remains legal in many countries'.
findings.truth: The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 suspended the death penalty for murder in Great Britain for five years; Parliament made it permanent in December 1969 (Northern Ireland 1973). It stayed on the statute book for treason and piracy with violence until the Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Capital punishment in the United Kingdom; Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965; Crime and Disorder Act 1998

findings.claim: Corporal punishment 'is banned in the UK but remains legal in some countries'.
findings.truth: It is banned in schools and cannot be imposed by a court, but physical punishment by a parent is still lawful in England and Northern Ireland. 'Banned in the UK' flat is not true.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, School corporal punishment - state schools 22 July 1986; independent schools England and Wales 1998, Scotland 2000, Northern Ireland 2003

findings.claim: 'The death penalty is a frequent 12-mark question topic'; 'Examiners test all three'; 'The 12-mark evaluation question often asks you to weigh these two principles against each other' (exam tip); and in lesson 5, 'key ethical concepts the examiners expect to see'.
findings.truth: None of these can be sourced. House rule forbids invented statements about what examiners set or reward. The advice itself is sound, so only the examiner framing is removed.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims; spec 3.2.1.5 names both ethical arguments

findings.claim: Item 4: 'The aim of punishment that focuses on helping criminals change their behaviour is called _____.' Options are retribution, deterrence, reformation, rehabilitation; 'reformation' is keyed correct.
findings.truth: Rehabilitation is a synonym of reformation here, so a student who understands the idea can be marked wrong. The distractor must be a different concept.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the answer key against the options

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 4: 'Islam - the Qur’an supports retribution as a principle of justice: ‘We ordained for them: a life for a life, an eye for an eye’ (5:45).'
findings.truth: Qur'an 5:45 reports a ruling given to the Children of Israel in the Torah. The lesson body states this carefully; the mark scheme dropped it and read as though the verse prescribes retribution for Muslims. The Qur'anic basis for qisas among Muslims is 2:178.

findings.claim: Gee Walker 'said: “I can’t hate. I have to forgive them. Unforgiveness makes you a victim, and I refuse to be a victim.”' A shortened form appears in the question 6 mark scheme.
findings.truth: Her documented words are 'I have to forgive them. I can't feel anger and hatred, because that is what killed my son.' The published sentence is a composite no source supports, put in the mouth of a living named person.

findings.claim: 'Anthony Walker ... was murdered in a racially motivated attack in Liverpool.' A knowledge check repeats 'in Liverpool in 2005'.
findings.truth: Anthony Walker, 18, was killed with an ice axe in Huyton, in the borough of Knowsley, Merseyside, on 29-30 July 2005. Huyton is not in Liverpool.

findings.claim: 'Both agree that forgiveness leads to reconciliation and is ultimately better for the individual and society.'
findings.truth: The same lesson says some Christians separate forgiveness from reconciliation, which 'may not always be possible or safe'. Forgiveness can open the way to reconciliation; it does not lead to it automatically.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 3 paragraph n9 and the reconciliation glossary entry

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 6: Tutu 'believed that “without forgiveness, there is no future”, reflecting Jesus’s teaching on reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19)'.
findings.truth: 2 Corinthians is a letter written by Paul. The ministry-of-reconciliation passage is Paul's teaching, not a saying of Jesus. A student could repeat the wrong attribution in an answer.

findings.claim: 'The Qur’an teaches, “Let them pardon and forgive ...” It also states, “Pardon each other’s faults and God will grant you honour.”' The second quotation is repeated as a Qur'an quotation in the question 6 mark scheme.
findings.truth: The honour saying is not in the Qur'an. It is a hadith - Sahih Muslim 2588, 'the servant who forgives, Allah adds to his respect'. A search of the Qur'an returns no such verse. The first quotation is Qur'an 24:22 and carried no reference.
findings.evidence: Sahih Muslim 2588; quran.com 24:22; quran.com search API returns no match for the honour wording

findings.claim: 'For 5-mark questions, remember you need two developed points with at least one reference to sacred writings.'
findings.truth: There is no 5-mark part. The extended AO1 question in each theme is worth 6 marks, which is how this lesson's own practice questions are labelled.

findings.claim: 'Give one religious beliefs about forgiveness.' (lesson 4) and 'Give one reasons why people are against the death penalty.' (lesson 5).
findings.truth: Neither sentence parses.

findings.claim: Card 4 front reads '” This means that if _____ do not forgive others, God will not forgive them either', answer 'Christians'.
findings.truth: The card is a broken cloze cut out of the lesson text, opening with a stray closing quotation mark. A cloze card with a single-word answer must ask a question beginning What / Which / Who / When / Name.

findings.claim: Four revision tips are garbled: 'Cover this box. Write down what you recall about jesus died on the cross for the forgiveness.'; 'Cover this box. Describe the process for forgiveness links closely to the step by step.'; 'Cover this box. Define the principle of utility says an action in your own words.' and 'Cover this box. Define under Shari’ah law, the death penalty in your own words.' (the last two in lesson 5).
findings.truth: Auto-generated text that does not read as English. Students see these tips on the key-fact boxes.

findings.claim: 'It was abolished in the UK in 1965 as a temporary measure and permanently abolished in 1969.' The key fact, the takeaways, a knowledge check and two flashcards repeat 'permanently abolished in the UK in 1969'.
findings.truth: The 1965 Act covered murder only. Treason and piracy with violence kept the death penalty until the Crime and Disorder Act 1998; the military offences went with the Human Rights Act 1998. 1969 made the ban on hanging for murder permanent.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Capital punishment in the United Kingdom - Commons 16 December 1969, Crime and Disorder Act 1998 in force 30 September 1998

findings.claim: Cards 4 and 5 read 'It was abolished in the UK in _____ as a temporary measure and permanently abolished in 1969' and 'Key Fact The death penalty was permanently abolished in the UK in _____'.
findings.truth: Both are broken clozes cut from the lesson text, one carrying the words 'Key Fact'. A single-word cloze answer needs a question beginning What / Which / Who / When / Name.

findings.claim: 'Life sentences do not always mean life - murderers in the UK walk free after an average of sixteen years.'
findings.truth: No published figure supports sixteen years. Recorded averages move year by year (14 years for mandatory lifers released in 2006; commonly quoted as 15-20 years since) and the minimum term set by the judge, not an average, is the rule a student can state.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Life imprisonment in England and Wales

findings.claim: 'The Ten Commandments teach “Do not kill” (Exodus 20:13)' - repeated in the takeaways, a matching knowledge check and three mark schemes.
findings.truth: Exodus 20:13 reads 'You shall not murder' (NIV, NRSV). Lesson 1 of this same unit quotes it correctly. The kill / murder wording is the crux of the death-penalty argument, so the misquotation is not cosmetic.

findings.claim: 'The Qur’an teaches “Whoever has spared a life, it is as though he has spared the life of all of mankind” (Surah 5:32).'
findings.truth: No published translation reads that way. The verse runs 'whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity'.

findings.claim: The 12-mark scheme ends 'Max L2 if no reference to religion' and names a 'Lower band (1-3)'.
findings.truth: 'L2' is a board level code that means nothing to a student and belongs to the board's own level wording. The house ladder runs Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band.
findings.evidence: house copyright-distancing rule and band vocabulary

findings.claim: 'I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn away from their ways and live' (Ezekiel 33:11), repeated in a mark scheme.
findings.truth: The NIV reads 'but rather that they turn from their ways and live'.

findings.claim: 'The Qur’an says “retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain.”' - no reference given.
findings.truth: The verse is 2:178, which sets retaliation for murder and then allows the victim's family to take blood money instead. The quoted wording matches no published translation.

findings.claim: 'Bentley was later given a posthumous pardon in 1998.'
findings.truth: Derek Bentley was granted a royal pardon on 29 July 1993; the Court of Appeal quashed his conviction on 30 July 1998. Two different acts, five years apart.

findings.claim: 'Under Shari’ah law, the death penalty is a hudud punishment for some crimes, meaning the Qur’an says it is compulsory. However, mercy is greatly valued - the victim’s family can accept “blood money” instead of execution.'
findings.truth: Hudud punishments are fixed and cannot be waived by a victim's family. Blood money belongs to qisas, the law on murder (Qur'an 2:178). Lesson 4 of this unit draws the distinction correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: quran.com 2:178; lesson 4 'Limits to Forgiveness in Islam'

findings.claim: Lesson 4 'Forgiveness' teaches the same spec point as lesson 3, which is titled 'Forgiveness & Corporal Punishment' and is entirely about forgiveness.
findings.truth: Two live lessons cover forgiveness with different framings: lesson 3 contrasts unconditional Christian forgiveness with an Islamic right to justice and uses Gee Walker, Tutu and the Amish; lesson 4 uses the hudud / al-jinayaat distinction with Maureen Greaves and the Iranian mother. Options: (a) keep lesson 4 as the teachings lesson and cut the duplicate half of lesson 3; (b) merge the case studies into one lesson and give the freed slot to corporal punishment, which no lesson teaches in its own right. Recommendation: (b) - the spec names corporal punishment as one of the three contrasting-belief issues, and it currently gets one paragraph inside lesson 2.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.5 - corporal punishment, death penalty and forgiveness are the three contrasting-beliefs issues

findings.claim: Lesson 5 'The Death Penalty' repeats the death-penalty half of lesson 2 'Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty'.
findings.truth: Both lessons teach the principle of utility, the sanctity of life, the arguments for and against, and the Christian and Muslim positions. They also disagree: lesson 2 says the death penalty was abolished in 1965, lesson 5 says 1969. Options: (a) leave both as revision overlap; (b) strip the death penalty out of lesson 2 so it covers aims and treatment of criminals only, leaving lesson 5 as the single death-penalty lesson. Recommendation: (b), which also removes the date clash.
findings.evidence: comparison of lesson 2 sections n11-n20 with lesson 5

findings.claim: Lesson 3 is titled 'Forgiveness & Corporal Punishment' but holds no corporal punishment content; corporal punishment appears only in lesson 2.
findings.truth: The title promises material the lesson does not hold. Title is not an editable field in this pass, so it is recorded only.

findings.claim: 'Since abolition in the UK, three people have been pardoned after new evidence proved they were innocent' - repeated in the key fact box.
findings.truth: The number cannot be verified. The recorded cases are not a tidy three and are not all pardons: Timothy Evans had a free pardon in 1966, Derek Bentley a royal pardon in 1993, while Mahmood Mattan (1998) and George Kelly (2003) had convictions quashed, which is not the same act. Options: (a) name the cases the lesson can support and drop the count; (b) keep the count only if a source is found. Recommendation: (a).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Capital punishment in the United Kingdom, and Derek Bentley case; no source found for a total of three

findings.claim: Lessons 1-3 of this bespoke Unity unit are word-for-word the same as lessons 1-3 of the free-tier unit religious-studies-aqa/theme-e-crime-punishment, apart from revision tips and flashcard decks. Those rows were fact-checked and corrected on 6 September 2026; these rows still carry every one of those errors.
findings.truth: The same lesson is live in two versions, one corrected and one not. The edits in this pass bring the Unity rows into line with the corrected free-tier wording. The wider question - how a bespoke school row came to hold generic text at all, given the rule that generic and school content never mix - is Tom's, not a fact-check matter.

findings.claim: 'Islamic law (Shari’ah) permits the death penalty for certain serious offences, including murder and apostasy.'
findings.truth: Classical Sunni jurisprudence does prescribe death for apostasy, so the statement is not false, but the ruling rests on hadith rather than the Qur'an and many contemporary scholars reject it. Stated flat, it reads as settled law.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.5 does not name apostasy; standard GCSE treatment

findings.claim: Allah is 'the most merciful' (Ar-Rahman) in lesson 1; Ar-Rahman ('the Most Merciful') in lesson 3.
findings.truth: Ar-Rahman is normally rendered 'the Most Gracious' or 'the Most Compassionate'; Ar-Rahim is 'the Most Merciful'. The gloss used here is common in GCSE textbooks, so it will not cost marks.

findings.claim: The 12-mark scheme names a 'Lower band (1-3)' and gives four band descriptors close to the board's own level wording.
findings.truth: The house ladder is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. Not on the validator's banned list, and the lesson 5 copy is corrected in this pass; recorded here so the two lessons can be brought into line in one sweep.

findings.claim: Question 3 asks for 'two similar religious beliefs in contemporary British society about why murder is wrong'.
findings.truth: The contrasting-beliefs question is set on the three named issues - corporal punishment, the death penalty and forgiveness - so a 4-mark beliefs question about murder is off-pattern. It is still useful practice, so no edit.

findings.claim: 'Do not take life, which Allah has made sacred, except by right' (Surah 17:33) and 'If anyone is killed unjustly, we have granted the right of retribution to his heir' (Surah 17:33).
findings.truth: The published translation of 17:33 reads 'God' where the lesson writes 'Allah', and the second half runs 'We have given his heir authority', which the lesson paraphrases. Both are close enough not to mislead.

findings.claim: 'The Old Testament teaches “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exodus 21:24)' - the NIV has no articles.
findings.truth: Checked and sound: the NLT reads 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot'. The quotation matches a recognised translation, so no edit.

summary: Five lessons, 39 findings, 50 edits. The damage is concentrated in the two Unity-only lessons: a hadith quoted as a Qur'an verse, a 5-mark question type that does not exist, three broken cloze flashcards, the death penalty called 'permanently abolished in 1969' with no mention of 1998, Exodus 20:13 quoted as 'Do not kill', Derek Bentley's pardon dated 1998 instead of 1993, and blood money attached to hudud instead of qisas. Lessons 1-3 are the same text as the free-tier unit corrected on 6 September, so the same corrections are applied here, plus four garbled revision tips and four invented examiner claims. Lessons 4 and 5 duplicate lessons 3 and 2 - recorded as ADJUDICATE, not edited.
